title: The Ark Among the Philistines
summary: The Philistines carry the captured ark to Ashdod and set it in the temple of their god Dagon as a trophy. Two mornings in a row they find Dagon fallen on his face before the ark, the second time with his head and hands broken off. The LORD's hand then strikes the people of Ashdod with tumors, and when the ark is moved to Gath and then Ekron, panic and plague follow it, until the Ekronites demand that it be sent back to Israel.
story: Chapter 4 ended in despair: the ark captured, Eli and his sons dead, and the glory gone from Israel. Chapter 5 shows what is happening on the other side of the border, where no Israelite is present. The Philistines think they have won a victory over Israel's God and placed him in submission to their own. The chapter overturns that assumption at every step. Without an Israelite army, priest, or prophet, the LORD defends his own honor, humbles the Philistine god, and afflicts the victors. It is the first demonstration in the book that the ark's capture was not God's defeat, and it leads directly to the ark's return in chapter 6.
historical:
Ashdod, Gath, and Ekron were three of the five chief Philistine cities, along with Gaza and Ashkelon. Ashdod lay near the coast; Ekron (identified with Tel Miqne) and Gath (identified with Tell es-Safi) lay further inland, closer to Israelite territory. All three have been excavated and show the distinctive material culture of the Philistines in the Iron Age. Each city was ruled by a lord, and the lords of the five cities acted together on matters of common concern, as they do here in deciding what to do with the ark.

Dagon was an ancient god of the wider Semitic world, not originally Philistine. He was worshiped in Mesopotamia and Syria long before the Philistines arrived, appearing in texts from Mari and Ugarit, and the Philistines evidently adopted him after settling in Canaan. Judges 16 places a temple of Dagon at Gaza, and much later, in the second century BC, 1 Maccabees 10 records that Jonathan the Maccabee burned the temple of Dagon at Ashdod. The note that the priests of Dagon still avoid stepping on the threshold to this day shows that the narrator knew of a continuing custom at that temple.
cultural:
In the ancient Near East, when one nation defeated another it often carried off the images of the defeated gods and placed them in the victor's temple, as a sign that the conquered god now served the victorious one. The Philistines treat the ark this way, setting it beside Dagon as a captured deity in attendance on their god. The image of Dagon falling face down before the ark reverses the picture: Dagon, not the LORD, is in the posture of a worshiper or a defeated vassal. The broken head and hands are significant, since in ancient art and practice cutting off the head and hands of a defeated enemy was a way of displaying total victory.

Thresholds were widely regarded as places of spiritual significance and danger in the ancient world, and customs about not stepping on them are attested among several peoples. Zephaniah 1:9 condemns those who leap over the threshold, which many take as a reference to a similar pagan practice. The affliction described as tumors is uncertain. The Hebrew word probably refers to swellings, and the mention of rats in chapter 6 has led many to suggest an outbreak of bubonic plague, which rodents spread and which produces swellings, though the text does not allow certainty.
literary: The chapter is built with a sharp sense of irony and something close to satire. The first scene (verses 1-5) is a two-morning sequence, in which the repetition (fallen on his face before the ark of the LORD) turns the scene into a comedy of a god who has to be picked up and set back in his place, and then cannot even stay whole. The second part (verses 6-12) follows the ark's route from Ashdod to Gath to Ekron like a hot object passed from hand to hand. The key word is hand: the LORD's hand is heavy on the people, and Dagon's hands lie broken on the threshold. The word heavy (from the same root as glory) also answers chapter 4. The glory had departed from Israel, but the LORD's weight is felt heavily among the Philistines. The chapter ends with the outcry of the city rising to heaven, echoing Israel's cry in Egypt.

outline.t: Dagon falls before the ark in Ashdod
The LORD's hand afflicts Ashdod; the ark moved to Gath
Ekron demands that the ark be sent back

doctrines.note: The chapter mocks the idea that a man-made image could stand before the living God. Dagon has to be lifted up and set in place by his worshipers, and he cannot protect himself. The Prophets later make the same point about idols that must be carried and cannot save (Isaiah 46:1-7).

God is sovereign beyond Israel's borders and apart from Israel's help. He acts in the heart of a pagan temple and across Philistine cities, showing that his rule does not depend on his people's military success.

The LORD's hand falls on the Philistines, not as random calamity but as a response to their treatment of him as a captured trophy. The pattern recalls the plagues of Egypt, where God judged a nation that held what belonged to him.

words.note: Dagon, the name of the god. Older interpreters linked the name to the Hebrew word for fish and pictured Dagon as a fish-god, but most scholars now relate it to the word for grain, dagan, and consider him a god associated with grain and fertility. The ancient texts from Syria support that view, and the fish interpretation is largely abandoned.

Yad, hand, often used for power or control. The chapter contrasts the LORD's heavy hand, which strikes cities, with Dagon's broken hands lying helpless on the threshold. The Israelites had been delivered into the hand of the Philistines, and now the Philistines discover whose hand is really strong.

Kavad, to be heavy, from the same root as kavod, glory. The chapter says the LORD's hand was heavy on Ashdod and Ekron. The echo of chapter 4 is deliberate: Ichabod's mother mourned that the glory had departed, but that glory, the weight of God's presence, is now pressing down on the Philistines.

Seren, lord or ruler, a title used in the Old Testament only for the rulers of the five Philistine cities. Its origin is debated; some scholars have linked it to a word from the Aegean or Anatolian world, in keeping with the Philistines' foreign roots, while others are more cautious.

christ: The chapter shows a God who defeats his enemies without help, at a moment when his people have lost everything. That pattern, of God acting alone to win a victory his people could not win, runs through the Bible and reaches its climax at the cross, where Jesus appears captured and defeated and yet triumphs over the powers arrayed against God. Paul describes this in Colossians 2:15, where Christ disarms the rulers and authorities and triumphs over them. The link is a matter of biblical theme, not prediction: 1 Samuel 5 does not speak of Christ, but it teaches readers to expect that God's apparent defeat may be the setting for his victory, a lesson the New Testament applies to the crucifixion.

hard.q: Is it fair that ordinary Philistine townspeople suffered because of what their rulers and army did with the ark?
hard.a: The plague strikes the men of the cities, young and old, not only the soldiers or rulers who captured the ark, and modern readers feel the problem. Several considerations are offered. The ancient world understood communities as bound together; the whole city had received the ark as a trophy of victory and shared in honoring Dagon above the LORD. The narrative also shows that the affliction ends when the ark is returned, which suggests its purpose was to make the Philistines acknowledge the LORD rather than to destroy them. Some readers stress that the Philistines had a clear way out and were not trapped. Others acknowledge that the text simply describes judgment falling broadly, as it often does in history, and that the Bible elsewhere wrestles openly with the suffering of the innocent. The chapter's main concern is the unmasking of a false god, but the question of collective judgment is a real one, and Scripture does not always resolve it neatly.

questions: The Philistines had to set Dagon back on his pedestal. What things do people rely on that have to be propped up by our own effort to stay standing?
God acted in this chapter without any help from Israel. How does it change your perspective to know that God's purposes do not depend on the success of his people?
The ark caused panic in each city it entered. What might it mean that God's presence is comforting to some and terrifying to others?
